strengths: The shared construction for forests and ReLU networks offers an understandable approach to reducing confidence far from training data. It has an identifiable audience among researchers studying uncertainty estimation and density-based classification.

The five controlled simulations, learning curves over 45 repetitions, and posterior visualizations provide useful evidence of reduced distant-OOD confidence in the balanced, two-dimensional settings studied. Classification performance is generally competitive at larger sample sizes.

The equations, pseudocode, and linked code repository help communicate the intended method. These contributions could support a useful, carefully scoped simulation paper. Source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-ep75gnq4/call-6398a4343f324bb4809eacf2527d788f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the central uniform-confidence claim. In Eqs. (3.6)–(3.8), when all Gaussian density estimates vanish, the posterior approaches the empirical class prior, not 1/K. A 90:10 training distribution therefore produces limiting confidence 0.9. The balanced experiments conceal this limitation. Furthermore, decay at infinity does not establish uniform confidence everywhere outside the training distribution’s support, as targeted by Eq. (2.1). Restrict the claims accordingly or revise and validate the inference rule.

Necessary: Support or remove the consistency assertion on page 2. No proof or sufficiently precise conditions establish convergence to the true distribution. Conditions governing partition refinement, neighborhood weights, and covariance estimates matter: a pure leaf can retain an entire non-Gaussian class distribution that one fitted Gaussian cannot recover. Sufficient classifier complexity alone does not establish the stated result.

Necessary: Align the performance claims with Figure 2. KDF has higher circle classification error than RF at smaller sample sizes, and both proposed methods have worse Gaussian-XOR Hellinger distances than their respective parents over substantial sample-size ranges. These observations contradict the statements that posterior estimates are 'always' better and that OOD detection entails no sacrifice of in-distribution performance. Describe the observed tradeoffs and the regimes where improvements occur.

Necessary: Resolve the method specification and supply essential parameters. Eq. (3.4) measures pre-activation discrepancies, whereas Algorithm 3, line 12, measures post-activation discrepancies; these generally produce different weights. The manuscript also omits the experimental values and selection procedures for C, h, and T, and how singular covariance estimates from sparsely populated neighborhoods are handled. These details affect both reproducibility and the confidence behavior.

Necessary: Clarify the evaluation protocol. Specify independent training and evaluation samples, neural-network stopping criteria, OOD sampling and sample counts, the detection score and FPR@95 convention, and how true posteriors and Hellinger distances were calculated. The Gaussian-XOR definition also gives identical mixture means for both classes, which would not generate the XOR structure shown in Figure 1. The repository link does not resolve these ambiguities within the supplied manuscript.

Necessary for retaining the human-intelligence conclusion: Figure 3 reports averaged class probabilities, but an average near 0.5 does not establish individual uncertainty; confidently opposing judgments can also average to 0.5. The selected 82-degree slice provides no uncertainty intervals or direct quantitative comparison with KDF/KDN. Analyze individual maximum confidence and variability across the test region, or limit the conclusion to the observed aggregate response pattern.

Optional: Compare with ordinary KDE using the same density floor and ablate the polytope weighting to identify what the learned partitions contribute. Runtime measurements and higher-dimensional applications would further clarify practical usefulness. The acceptance concerns above concern correctness, evidential scope, and reproducibility; they do not require state-of-the-art performance.
